title: Tournai to Paris: the Making of France
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Cradle of the Sicambrians, Tournai

stops.name: Tournai, the hall of Childeric, king of the Salian Franks
stops.campa: A son is born to Childeric in the old Roman city on the Scheldt, and to Basina his queen, who left the king of Thuringia because she knew Childeric to be the strongest man in the world. On the first night she bids the king rise and look out from the hall, and he sees lions, unicorns and leopards walking; the second night bears and wolves; the third, dogs and lesser beasts tearing one another: the generations of the long-haired kings shown in order, and the lion at the head of them is this child, Clovis.
suggested_refs: the long-haired kings of the Merovingians
sources: Fredegar, Chronicle III.12
Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.12, II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I

stops.name: Tournai, Saint-Brice, the tomb of Childeric
stops.campa: Childeric is laid in the earth by the church of Saint-Brice with his warhorses about him, his cloisonné sword, the crystal ball, the signet ring cut CHILDIRICI REGIS, and three hundred golden bees with garnet wings sewn to his cloak. The mound closes over the pagan splendor and sleeps eleven hundred years, until 27 May 1653, when the mason Adrien Quinquin's pick breaks the chamber and the bees swarm out of history: Chifflet engraves them for the Archduke, and Napoleon sews them onto his coronation mantle in place of the Bourbon lily.
suggested_refs: the golden bees of Childeric (Bibliothèque nationale, Cabinet des Médailles)
sources: Jean-Jacques Chifflet, Anastasis Childerici I Francorum regis (1655)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childeric_I
https://penelope.uchicago.edu/hydrionoframes/bees.xhtml

stops.name: Tournai, Clovis raised king at fifteen
stops.campa: Childeric dies and Clovis his son reigns in his stead. He is fifteen years old. The Salian warriors lift the boy on the shield after the custom of the Franks and carry him about the assembly; the long hair of the kings falls to his shoulders, which no razor may touch while he rules. Around him the map is broken pieces: Syagrius the Roman at Soissons, Ragnachar at Cambrai, Chararic beyond, Sigibert the Lame at Cologne, Goths south of the Loire, Burgundians on the Rhône. He will gather every piece.
suggested_refs: the royal long hair of the Merovingians
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I

segments.name: The Last Roman Island: Soissons and the Vase

stops.name: Soissons, the field against Syagrius
stops.campa: In the fifth year of his reign Clovis marches on Syagrius, king of the Romans, son of Aegidius, who holds his seat at Soissons, the last island of Rome in the drowned province. With him comes his kinsman Ragnachar; Chararic stands at a distance, waiting to befriend the victor, and that waiting will be remembered. Clovis demands that a battlefield be made ready, and Syagrius does not delay nor fear to resist. The lines meet; the Roman army is crushed; Syagrius turns his back and flees swiftly to Alaric at Toulouse. Rome in Gaul is ended.
suggested_refs: the kingdom of Soissons, last Roman enclave
Aegidius and the domain of Syagrius
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Soissons_(486)

stops.name: Soissons, the division of the plunder and the vase
stops.campa: The army, still in heathen error, has despoiled the churches, and among the booty is a vase of wonderful size and beauty. The bishop sends messengers begging that at least the vase be returned, and the king answers: follow us to Soissons, where all is divided by lot. There, before the heaped plunder, he asks his warriors for the ewer above his share. The wiser consent: all we see is yours. But a foolish, envious and excitable fellow lifts his battle-axe and splits it, crying that the king shall have nothing but what the lot fairly bestows. Clovis carries the wound in silence one whole year.
stops.quote: I ask of you, brave warriors, not to refuse to grant me in addition to my share, yonder dish.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vase_of_Soissons

stops.name: Toulouse, Syagrius surrendered in chains
stops.campa: Clovis sends word to Alaric, king of the Goths: give the Roman back, or know that the Franks will make war for the refusal. Alaric is afraid to incur the anger of the Franks on Syagrius' account, it is the fashion of the Goths to be terrified, Gregory writes, and he surrenders his guest bound to the envoys. Clovis puts him under guard, and when the kingdom of Soissons is fully his, he orders him executed in secret. The Gothic king who gave up a suppliant will himself be given up, at Vouillé, to the point of Clovis' own spear.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syagrius

stops.name: Soissons, the Field of March, the axe answered
stops.campa: At the end of the year the army assembles in arms on the Field of March for the review of weapons. The king walks the ranks and comes to the man who struck the vase. No one, he says, has brought armor so ill-kept, neither spear nor sword nor axe serviceable, and he seizes the man's axe and casts it down. As the soldier bends to pick it up, the king drives his own axe into his skull, and orders the rest to depart, raising great dread of himself. It is the founding parable of Frankish kingship: what the king claims, no lot may deny.
stops.quote: This is what you did at Soissons to the vase.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: the Champ de Mars muster of the Franks
the francisca, the throwing-axe of the Franks
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vase_of_Soissons

stops.name: The Thuringian country, the tenth-year war (traditional seat on the Unstrut)
stops.campa: In the tenth year of his reign he makes war on the Thuringians and brings them under his dominion. The canon gives the campaign one sentence, as a smith gives one hammer-blow; behind it the host crosses the Rhine into his mother Basina's country and returns with the east made quiet. He has broken the Roman island and now the German marches; he has made many wars and gained many victories, and he is not yet thirty. The kingdoms around him begin to send embassies, and among the embassies goes one to Burgundy.
suggested_refs: the Thuringian kingdom of the Unstrut
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.27 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuringii

segments.name: The Burgundian Bride, Geneva to Soissons

stops.name: Geneva, Clotilde found in exile
stops.campa: Gundobad of Burgundy has killed his brother Chilperic with the sword and drowned Chilperic's wife with a stone tied to her neck; of the two daughters, Chrona has taken the nun's habit, and the younger, Clotilde, lives at Geneva serving the poor and washing the feet of pilgrims. Clovis' envoys, sent often into Burgundy, find the maiden and see that she is of good bearing and wise, and learn she is of royal blood. Aurelian comes to her disguised as a beggar; kneeling as she washes his feet, he shows her the ring of the Frankish king, and she accepts it in secret.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
Fredegar, Chronicle III.18-19
Liber Historiae Francorum 11-12

stops.name: Soissons, the marriage of Clovis and Clotilde
stops.campa: Clovis sends to Gundobad asking Clotilde in marriage, and Gundobad, not daring to refuse, gives her over to the envoys. On the road she leaves the slow ox-cart and rides ahead on horseback, urging haste before her uncle repents of the gift. Clovis receives her with great joy and marries her at Soissons. She is the Christian princess who will not relent: from the marriage bed she begins her long siege of the king's soul, telling him that the idols he honors are nothing, wood and stone and metal, and that he should honor instead the God who made heaven and earth.
suggested_refs: Saint Clotilde, queen of the Franks
the ox-cart left on the Burgundian road
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
Fredegar, Chronicle III.18-19
Liber Historiae Francorum 12

stops.name: Soissons, Ingomer dies in his white robes
stops.campa: The queen makes her firstborn ready for baptism, adorning the church with hangings and curtains, that the king who cannot be moved by persuasion might be urged by the mystery. The boy, named Ingomer, is baptized, and dies still wearing the white garments of his regeneration. The king is violently angry: had the child been dedicated to his gods, he would live. The queen does not bend. She gives thanks to the omnipotent God who judged her not wholly unworthy, that one born of her womb should be taken, in his baptismal robes, into the kingdom of God.
stops.quote: If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods he would certainly have lived; but as it is, since he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live at all.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: the death in albis, the baptismal whites
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Soissons, Chlodomer saved by the queen's prayer
stops.campa: A second son is born and named Chlodomer at his baptism, and he too falls sick. The king's bitterness speaks first: this one will die like his brother, baptized in the name of your Christ. But through the prayers of his mother, and at the Lord's command, the child becomes well. It is the first miracle granted inside the king's own house, and it is Clotilde's: the pagan king watches his son live and says nothing, and the queen does not cease urging him to know the true God and to leave the idols that can help neither themselves nor anyone.
stops.quote: It is impossible that anything else should happen to him than happened to his brother, namely, that being baptized in the name of your Christ, should die at once.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

segments.name: The Vow and the Font, Tolbiac to Reims

stops.name: Tolbiac (Zülpich), the vow on the battlefield
stops.campa: In the fifteenth year of his reign war comes with the Alamanni, and in the fierce slaughter the Frankish line begins to break. Clovis sees his army in danger of destruction, raises his eyes to heaven, and with remorse in his heart bursts into tears and cries his vow to the God of Clotilde. As the words leave him, the Alamanni turn their backs and scatter; their king is killed, and the people submit, praying that no more perish: we are yours now. He stops the killing and rides home to tell the queen how Christ gave the victory. His Constantine moment; the bridge is Tolbiac.
stops.quote: Jesus Christ, whom Clotilda asserts to be the son of the living God, who art said to give aid to those in distress, and to bestow victory on those who hope in thee, I beseech the glory of thy aid, with the vow that if thou wilt grant me victory over these enemies, and I shall know that power which she says that people dedicated in thy name have had from thee, I will believe in thee and be baptized in thy name. For I have invoked my own gods but, as I find, they have withdrawn from aiding me; and therefore I believe that they possess no power, since they do not help those who obey them. I now call upon thee, I desire to believe thee, only let me be rescued from my adversaries.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.30 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: the Battle of Tolbiac (Ary Scheffer's painting, Versailles)
the Constantine parallel at the Milvian Bridge
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.30 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tolbiac

stops.name: Reims, the secret instruction by Saint Remigius
stops.campa: The queen asks Saint Remi, bishop of Reims, to summon the king secretly and open to him the word of salvation. The bishop urges him to believe in the true God, maker of heaven and earth, and to cease worshipping idols that help no one. The king hears gladly but fears his people will not abandon their gods; he will go and speak to them. He meets his followers, and before he can open his mouth the power of God anticipates him: all the people cry out together, O pious king, we reject our mortal gods, and we are ready to follow the immortal God whom Remi preaches.
stops.quote: I gladly hear you, most holy father; but there remains one thing: the people who follow me cannot endure to abandon their gods; but I shall go and speak to them according to your words.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Reims, the baptism at Christmas, three thousand behind him
stops.campa: The squares are shaded with tapestried canopies, the churches hung with white curtains; incense spreads, fragrant candles burn, and the baptistery fills with such perfume that the bystanders believe themselves amid the odors of paradise. The king asks to be baptized first: a new Constantine advances to the font to wash away the old leprosy. Remigius speaks the sentence over the bowed Sicambrian; Clovis, confessing God in Trinity, is anointed with chrism. More than three thousand of his army follow, and his sisters Albofled and Lantechild. In this same church the Maid will stand with her banner beside the Dauphin she crowns: his Reims faces Joan's.
stops.quote: Gently bend your neck, Sigamber; worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: the Baptism of Clovis (Master of Saint Giles, National Gallery of Art)
Joan of Arc at the coronation of Charles VII, 17 July 1429
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism_of_Clovis

stops.name: Reims, Saint-Remi, the dove and the Holy Ampulla
stops.campa: The press of the crowd in the streets is so great that the clerk bearing the chrism cannot reach the font, and the holy oil is kept away. Remigius lifts his eyes, and a dove whiter than snow descends bearing in its beak a little vial of chrism sent from heaven; a fragrance beyond all incense fills the church, and with this oil the king is anointed. The vial is the Sainte Ampoule, kept at Saint-Remi: for thirteen hundred years it anoints the kings of France, down to the Dauphin whom Joan crowns in 1429 and the last king at Reims in 1825.
suggested_refs: the Sainte Ampoule (basilica of Saint-Remi, Reims)
the coronation ordo of the kings of France
sources: Hincmar of Reims, Vita Remigii (MGH SRM III)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Ampulla

segments.name: The Burgundian War: the Ouche and the Rhône

stops.name: Dijon, on the river Ouche, the brothers' battle
stops.campa: Godegisel, weary of his brother Gundobad's kingship, promises Clovis tribute in secret if he will help destroy him. Gundobad, ignorant of the treachery, calls his brother to his side against the Franks, and the three armies converge on the stronghold called Dijon. They fight on the Ouche; Godegisel goes over to Clovis in the midst of the battle, and together they crush Gundobad's people. Gundobad, seeing the treason of the brother he never suspected, turns and flees down the valley of the Rhône to shut himself in Avignon, while Godegisel enters Vienne in triumph as if the whole kingdom were already his.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.32 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gundobad

stops.name: Avignon, the siege turned by the counsel of Aridius
stops.campa: Clovis sits with all his army around the walls, meaning to drag Gundobad out and slay him. But Gundobad's man Aridius, famed for energy and wisdom, feigns desertion and comes to the Frankish king, who keeps him close, for he is entertaining in storytelling, ready in counsel, just in judgment. Then, softly, Aridius talks the siege away: why hold an army against a strong place, ravaging fields you cannot eat? Clovis takes the advice, imposes a yearly tribute, and marches home. Gundobad pays, for a while, then besieges Godegisel in Vienne and kills him in an Arian church. Burgundy waits a generation for Clotilde's sons.
stops.quote: Send an embassy rather and impose tribute to be paid you every year, so that the country may be safe and you may rule forever over a tributary. And if he refuses, then do whatever pleases you.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.32 (trans. Brehaut), the counsel of Aridius
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.32-33 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

segments.name: The War of God: the Road to Vouillé

stops.name: The island of the Loire at Amboise, the two kings meet
stops.campa: Alaric, king of the Goths, watching Clovis conquer nations steadily, sends envoys asking for a meeting. Clovis does not spurn it. The two kings come to an island of the Loire near the village of Amboise in the territory of Tours, and there they talk and eat and drink together, plight friendship, and depart in peace. It is the peace of two swordsmen measuring the ground. Even at that time, Gregory writes, many in the Gauls desired greatly to have the Franks as masters: the Catholic south already leaning toward the baptized king across the river.
stops.quote: If my brother consents, it is the desire of my heart that with God's favor we have a meeting.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.35 (trans. Brehaut), Alaric's message
suggested_refs: the Loire as frontier between Frank and Goth
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.35 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaric_II

stops.name: Paris, the word against the Arians
stops.campa: Clovis speaks to his people the sentence that launches the conquest of Aquitaine: it grieves him that Arians hold a part of the Gauls. The words please them all. The army is set in motion toward Poitiers, where Alaric waits. In the register of the canon this is not politics but crusade before the word exists: the king baptized at Reims goes down against the heretic kingdom with the favor of God marching before him in signs: a psalm, a hind, a pillar of fire, each about to be given in its place.
stops.quote: I take it very hard that these Arians hold part of the Gauls. Let us go with God's help and conquer them and bring the land under our control.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: The border of Touraine, the edict of Saint Martin
stops.campa: As the host passes into Touraine, the king issues an edict out of respect for the blessed Martin: no one shall take anything from this country but grass for fodder and water. A soldier finds a poor man's hay and reasons like a lawyer: did not the king say grass? and is not hay grass? He takes it by force. Quicker than speech the man is slain by the sword, and the king speaks his fear over the body: the victory itself hangs on Martin's goodwill. It would be better, he says, for the army to take nothing at all from this country.
stops.quote: And where shall our hope of victory be if we offend the blessed Martin?
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: Saint Martin of Tours, patron of the Franks
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Tours, basilica of Saint Martin, the omen of the psalm
stops.campa: The king sends envoys with gifts to the blessed church: go, he says, and perhaps you will receive some omen of victory from the holy temple, and he prays that if the Lord is his helper, He will consent to reveal it at the entrance. As the messengers step through the door of Saint Martin's, the first singer, without any pre-arrangement, lifts exactly this response into the air. They pay their vow to the blessed confessor and ride joyfully to the king: the omen is given, the unbelieving nation is surrendered into his hands.
stops.quote: Thou hast girded me, O Lord, with strength unto the battle; thou hast subdued under me those that rose up against me, and hast made mine enemies turn their backs unto me, and thou hast utterly destroyed them that hated me.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut), the response sung at the door of Saint Martin's
suggested_refs: the basilica of Saint Martin, Tours
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: The ford of the Vienne, the hind shows the crossing (traditional site by Vieux-Poitiers)
stops.campa: The army comes to the river Vienne and cannot cross: the rains have swollen it and no man knows the ford. In the night the king prays to the Lord to show him a way over. In the morning, by God's will, a hind of wonderful size enters the river before the host, and where she passes the people see the shallow path and cross behind her, dry-shouldered, to the Poitiers bank. The God who parted a sea for Israel parts a river for the Franks with the body of a deer.
suggested_refs: the Gué de Cenon by Vieux-Poitiers
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Before Poitiers, the fire from Saint-Hilaire
stops.campa: Encamped within sight of Poitiers, the king in the night sees a ball of fire come out of the church of Saint Hilarius and pass, as it were, over him: the light of the blessed confessor, who in his lifetime fought the Arian heresy with the pen, now goes before the army that will fight it with iron. Clovis makes it known to the whole host that neither here nor on the road shall any man spoil or take another's property: the discipline of Touraine renewed on the eve of battle, so that no offense may dim the light that has chosen him.
suggested_refs: Hilary of Poitiers, hammer of the Arians
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Vouillé, the campus Vogladensis, Alaric slain by the king's hand
stops.campa: On the field of Vouillé, at the tenth milestone from Poitiers, the armies meet: the Goths fight from a distance with darts, the Franks press in with the sword, and the Goths flee as is their custom. Clovis wins the victory, God helping him, and kills Alaric the king with his own hand. As he strikes, two Goths come at him suddenly with lances from either side, but his cuirass and his swift horse deliver him from death. Aquitaine is won in an afternoon; Amalaric, Alaric's son, flees to Spain; the Gothic kingdom of Toulouse is finished.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
Chronicle of Saragossa, s.a. 507
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vouill%C3%A9

stops.name: Bordeaux, the winter quarters
stops.campa: The king winters in Bordeaux, the Garonne city of the Goths now a Frankish court. From here he orders the reduction of the south: his son Theodoric is sent by way of Albi and Rodez to Clermont, and brings under his father's dominion the cities from the boundary of the Goths to the limit of the Burgundians. The map of France is being drawn this winter, road by road, in the itineraries of a nineteen-year-old prince and the garrisons of a baptized army.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Toulouse, the treasure of Alaric
stops.campa: Clovis enters Toulouse and takes all the treasures of Alaric: the hoard of the Balt kings, gathered since the sack of Rome a century before, wagonloads of the south's gold going north under Frankish spears. The city where Syagrius was surrendered in chains twenty-one years ago now surrenders everything. The kingdom that reigned in Toulouse for ninety years is carried away in its own coffers.
suggested_refs: the royal treasure of the Visigoths
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigothic_Kingdom

stops.name: Angoulême, the walls fall of their own accord
stops.campa: The king comes to Angoulême, and the Lord gives him such grace that the walls fall down of their own accord when he gazes at them. No engines, no ladders: the city opens like Jericho before the new Joshua. He drives out the Goths and takes the town under his own dominion, and with this the victory is complete. He turns north for Tours, bringing many gifts for the holy church of the blessed Martin, whose goodwill he guarded with an edict and whose psalm girded him for the battle.
suggested_refs: the Jericho figure in Frankish historiography
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

segments.name: The Purple at Tours, the Seat at Paris

stops.name: Tours, Saint Martin's, consul and Augustus
stops.campa: Letters come from the emperor Anastasius at Constantinople conferring the consulship. In the church of the blessed Martin the king clothes himself in the purple tunic and the chlamys and sets a diadem on his head; then he mounts his horse and rides from the gate of Saint Martin's atrium to the cathedral, scattering gold and silver among the people with his own hand along the whole way. From that day he is called consul or Augustus. The barbarian king wears Rome's colors in Martin's own house: the old empire hands its western title to the new France.
suggested_refs: Anastasius I, emperor of the East
the basilica of Saint Martin, Tours
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.38 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://edgyhistorian.blogspot.com/2017/09/gregory-of-tours-angers-consularia-and.html

stops.name: Paris, the seat of the kingdom
stops.campa: Leaving Tours he goes to Paris, and there he establishes the seat of his kingdom: the island city of the Parisii in its river, Geneviève's city; the shepherdess who turned Attila aside still lives within its walls to see the Frank make it a capital. Theodoric his son comes to him there. From this decision the whole shape of France descends: whatever the kingdom will be, it will be governed from this island, and the kings of a thousand years will reign where Clovis set his chair.
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.38 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I

segments.name: The Removal of the Kings and the Sleep at Paris

stops.name: Cologne, Sigibert, Chloderic, and the treasure chest
stops.campa: From Paris, Clovis sends secretly to the son of Sigibert the Lame: your father is old and limps on his weak foot; if he should die, his kingdom and our friendship would come to you. Chloderic has his father murdered as he sleeps at midday in the forest of Buchaw, and Clovis' envoys, come to view the dead king's treasure, bid him plunge his hand to the bottom of the chest. As he bends far over, an axe splits his skull. Then Clovis comes to Cologne, spreads his hands in innocence before the people, and they raise him on the shield and make him king.
stops.quote: I cannot shed the blood of my own kinsmen, which it is a crime to do. But since this has happened, I give you my advice, if it seems acceptable; turn to me, that you may be under my protection.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.40 (trans. Brehaut), Clovis to the people of Cologne
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.40 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Thérouanne, Chararic tonsured and slain (traditional seat)
stops.campa: Now he turns to Chararic, who at Soissons stood at a distance waiting to befriend the victor. Clovis entraps him with his son, imprisons them, and has them tonsured, the shears through the royal hair are a deposition deeper than death, ordaining the father priest and the son deacon. Chararic weeps at his degradation, and his son speaks the words that doom them: green wood sprouts. Word comes to Clovis that they mean to let their hair grow and kill him, and he orders both put to death, and takes their kingdom with the treasures and people.
stops.quote: It was on green wood that these twigs were cut, and they are not altogether withered. They will shoot out quickly, and be able to grow; may he perish as swiftly who has done this.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.41 (trans. Brehaut), the son of Chararic
suggested_refs: the tonsure as deposition of Merovingian kings
the long hair of the reges criniti
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.41 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Cambrai, Ragnachar, Ricchar, and the false gold
stops.campa: Ragnachar of Cambrai, unbridled in everything, his vile counselor Farro at his ear, is sold before the battle begins: Clovis has bought his leudes with arm-bands and sword-belts of gold: gilded bronze, false to the core. Beaten in the field, Ragnachar is seized by his own men and brought bound before Clovis with his brother Ricchar. The king reproaches him for disgracing their blood by suffering bonds, and the axe falls; to Ricchar: had you aided your brother, he would not have been bound, and the axe again. The betrayers discover their gold is counterfeit; such gold, says the king, as traitors deserve.
stops.quote: Why have you humiliated our family in permitting yourself to be bound? It would have been better for you to die.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: Rignomer, the third brother, slain at Le Mans
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Paris, the lament that is a trap
stops.campa: Having killed many other kings and his nearest relatives, jealous lest they take the kingdom from him, he has extended his rule over all the Gauls. Now he gathers his people together and mourns aloud the kinsmen he himself destroyed, a stranger among foreigners with no kin to help him in adversity. But he says this not from grief, Gregory records, but as a ruse: if perchance some relative still lives, the lament may draw him out of hiding to be killed. None comes. The chronicler writes down the cunning without blinking, and adds that God was laying the king's enemies low because he walked with an upright heart.
stops.quote: Woe to me, who have remained as a stranger among foreigners, and have none of my kinsmen to give me aid if adversity comes.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut)
suggested_refs: Gregory's epitaph on the consolidation: 'God was laying his enemies low every day under his hand'
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)

stops.name: Orléans, the first council of the Frankish church
stops.campa: By order of the king, thirty-two bishops of Gaul assemble at Orléans, five metropolitans among them, Cyprian of Bordeaux presiding, the bishops of the conquered Gothic south sitting beside those of the old Frankish north for the first time under one crown. They pass thirty-one canons on sanctuary, on church property, on the ordination of clerics, and send their decrees to the absent king for his confirmation, addressing him as the son of the catholic Church. The alliance of throne and altar that will carry France to 1789 is drafted here, in one July session, four months before the king dies.
stops.quote: To their lord, the son of the catholic Church, the most glorious king Clovis: all the bishops whom you have commanded to come to the council.
stops.quote_source: Acta of the First Council of Orléans (511), salutation of the synodal letter (MGH Concilia I)
sources: Acta of the First Council of Orléans, 511 (MGH Concilia I)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Orl%C3%A9ans
https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11318a.htm

stops.name: Paris, the death of the king
stops.campa: After all this he dies at Paris, in the fifth year after the battle of Vouillé. All the days of his reign are thirty years, and his age is forty-five. Gregory sets the mark of the saint on the span of the king: from the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Clovis, in the eleventh year of the episcopate of Licinius of Tours, one hundred and twelve years are reckoned: the history of Gaul measured from confessor to convert. The kingdom is divided among his four sons, Theodoric, Chlodomer, Childebert and Chlothar, and the story of France begins its long argument among heirs.
suggested_refs: the four sons and the first partition of Francia
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I

stops.name: Paris, the Church of the Holy Apostles on Sainte-Geneviève's hill, the burial
stops.campa: He is buried in the church of the Holy Apostles, which he himself built together with his queen Clotilde on the hill above the left bank, the hill that will take Geneviève's name when the saint of Paris is laid beside the king. Clotilde goes to Tours and serves in the church of Saint Martin with the greatest chastity and kindness all the days of her life, rarely visiting Paris; she outlives him by thirty-four years. His Reims faces Joan's Reims; his purple faces Charlemagne's crown; the line runs from this tomb through Martel to the empire, and every king of France is anointed with his Christmas oil.
suggested_refs: the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève (site by Saint-Étienne-du-Mont and the Lycée Henri-IV)
the tomb effigy of Clovis (basilica of Saint-Denis)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43 (trans. Brehaut, Fordham sourcebook)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_of_St_Genevieve
